title: Revealing relationships between porosity, microstructure and mechanical properties of laser powder bed fusion 316L stainless steel through heat treatment
body_text:
ABSTRACT

Laser powder bed fusion 316L samples are heat treated and characterised. • Microstructural features are related to anisotropic yield behaviour. • Anisotropic ductility is related to the shape, size and orientation of porosity. • Heat treatments are categorised by recovery, homogenisation and annealing regimes.

BODY

## Introduction

Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) produces unique microstructures which can compete favourably with other manufacturing

In the case of 316L stainless steel, LPBF manufactured material in the as-built state is often significantly stronger than traditionally manufactured material and may also achieve high ductility. LPBF material is generally anisotropic with both strength and ductility approximately 10% greater in the build plane (horizontal) than the build direction (vertical) in the as-built state. These properties are often attributed to microstructural features, but the individual contribution of each type of feature remains unclear.

The microstructure of as-built LPBF 316L is complex due to the intensity and speed of the heat source which induces large thermal gradients and non-equilibrium solidification structures. It is characterised by overlapping melt pools and columnar grains aligned with the build direction and containing fine subgranular cellular structures. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analyses have found grains to be around 10-500 lm long, and each grain contains a substructure of parallel cells approximately 500 nm wide that reveal the grain's solidification direction by their orientation. Cell walls contain higher concentrations of chromium and molybdenum than the cells' interiors, as well as higher dislocation densities. The misorientation between cells in a grain is very small (<1 • ), but between different grains the misorientation can be any angle. Grain boundaries and cell walls inhibit dislocation movement and thus strengthen the material.

Traces of scan tracks are revealed by bands of segregated solutes known as melt pool boundaries. These reflect the borders of adjacent scan tracks within the same layer (track-track) and between layers (layer-layer). Grains often protrude through layer boundaries indicating epitaxial grain growth, particularly when the local thermal gradient aligns with a preferred growth direction in the solid crystal. Melt pool boundaries are suspected of being weak regions of the material as failure along melt pool boundaries has been observed.

The largest phase by volume apart from austenite in LPBF 316L is gas inside pores. Although porosity is generally undesirable and considered a material defect rather than a feature, it will nonetheless remain important for LPBF part qualification in the foreseeable future. Porosity is generated by a variety of mechanisms including lack of fusion, keyhole-mode melting and gas absorption. No authoritative standard exists to qualify LPBF materials, but there is growing consensus that at least 99.5% of theoretical density is required to qualify as 'highly dense'. Relative density can be determined by a number of methods including the Archimedes method, image analysis of polished sections and X-ray computed tomography techniques.

The aim of this work is to clarify the relationships between porosity, microstructure and mechanical properties in LPBF 316L. Porosity was characterised by image analysis of large sections to determine the distribution of shape, size and orientation of pores and relative density of samples. The influence of microstructural features was investigated by subjecting samples to heat treatments designed to gradually dissolve these features. Through metallography and tensile testing of samples built in different orientations, the relative contribution of different features could be assessed. Sections of tensile samples tested to failure were analysed to evaluate the effects of microstructural features and porosity on failure behaviour.

## Materials and experimental methods

## Sample production and heat treatment

Test samples for this study were produced in a commercial Renishaw AM250 LPBF machine using manufacturer-recommended process parameters. 316L powder was supplied by LPW Technology Ltd. which consisted of 15-45 lm spherical particles of the nominal composition given in Table 1. Cylinders 70 mm long by 10 mm diameter were built with their axis in vertical (along the build direction) and horizontal (normal to the build direction) orientations on 5 mm supports in argon atmosphere (see Fig. 1). The pulsing 200 W laser was focused to a 65 lm spot. Points on the powder bed separated by 60 lm were exposed for 80 ls, giving the process an approximate scanning speed of 750 mm/s. The hatch spacing and layer thickness were 110 lm and 50 lm respectively. The 'chessboard' scanning strategy was used with 67 • rotation of the scanning direction between layers for most samples while a small set was produced using the 'meander' strategy with no rotation between layers. Upon completion of the build, the cylinders were removed from the build plate by cutting through the support structures.

Samples were subjected to varying levels of heat treatment ranging from no post-processing (the 'as-built' condition) to an annealing treatment expected to fully recrystallise the microstructure. These isothermal heat treatments were conducted in a Nabertherm N 41/H chamber furnace. Samples were placed in the preheated furnace filled with air and held for 60 min before being moved to ambient conditions and allowed to cool in air to room temperature. The holding temperatures were 700 • C, 800 • C, 900 • C, 1040 • C and 1200 • C, the latter representing full annealing. These temperatures were set and measured using the furnace temperature controller.

## Metallography and porosity analysis

As-built and heat treated samples were sectioned to examine horizontal and vertical surfaces in both build orientations as illustrated in Fig. 1. The four surfaces are labelled 'HH', 'HV', 'VH' and 'VV', where the first letter indicates the build orientation of the sample and the second letter is the section plane orientation. Sectioned samples were mounted in epoxy castings and ground flat with SiC grinding papers. Mechanical polishing with diamond suspensions down to 1 lm was followed by final polishing using 0.06 lm colloidal silica suspension. The samples were electrolytically etched in 10% oxalic acid solution applying a potential difference of 5 V for 90 s to reveal the microstructure. Etched samples were examined in a Zeiss Axioscope optical microscope and a Hitachi S-3400N scanning electron microscope (SEM). Applying an accelerating voltage of 13 kV at around 8 mm working distance produced a good signal for the backscattered electron (BSE) detector in the SEM. Material porosity was characterised by image analysis of polished surfaces. Samples were imaged and digitally stitched together to extend the field of view using a Hirox RH-2000 digital microscope at a resolution of 2.61 lm/pixel. A total area of at least 1000 mm 2 was imaged of each section shown in Fig. 1 to attain a statistically significant sample size of pores to be analysed. The composite images were analysed in ImageJ software. Area, fit ellipse and Feret's diameter parameters were recorded for each pore using the 'Analyse Particles' function. Objects smaller than 25 lm 2 (<4 pixels) were filtered out to exclude sample preparation artefacts from the data. The distribution of size, shape and orientation of pores and area fraction porosity was calculated in each orientation. The representative size of each pore was estimated by the mean of Feret's diameter, maximum fit ellipse length and root of area. Volumetric relative density was estimated by the geometric mean of area fraction porosity in horizontal (f H ) and vertical (f V ) sections of each sample using Eq. ( 1). The geometric mean is more conservative than the arithmetic as it gives greater weight to the section with more porosity.

## Tensile testing and post-test examination

Cylinders in as-built and heat treated conditions were machined into circular tensile specimens of 20 mm gauge length and 4.0 mm diameter in accordance with tolerances described in ASTM standard E8/E8 M. Samples were speckled using spray paint prior to testing so strain could be measured by digital image correlation (DIC) using the point-to-point method (virtual extensometer). Tensile testing to failure was conducted quasistatically at a strain rate not exceeding 5 • 10 -4 s -1. The gauge surface was photographed every 2 s using a 200 mm macro lens attached to a DSLR camera. The images were processed in GOM Correlate DIC software to calculate nominal engineering strain. Tests were repeated at least twice for each condition (orientation and heat treatment).

A post-test examination of fractured tensile samples was conducted by cold mounting and grinding samples with SiC papers to section the fracture surface longitudinally. These samples were polished and etched to reveal the microstructure near the fracture surface. The deformed subsurface microstructure was imaged using the Hirox RH-2000 digital microscope and Zeiss Axioscope optical microscope.

## Results and discussion

## Image analysis and porosity characterisation

Fig. 2 shows representative areas of polished samples used for porosity analysis. The larger pores in all samples were irregularly shaped and some contained powder particles, meaning they can be characterised as lack of fusion pores. Table 2 presents key results from the image analyses to characterise porosity in each build orientation. Note that the total area analysed for each section is much larger than the representative sections shown in Fig. 2 (see total area column in Table 2). A large cross-sectional area was required to produce adequate statistics to characterise porosity.

The pores were sorted by size into 10 lm intervals to produce the size distribution plots presented in Fig. 3. The top row shows histograms of pore size frequency while the plots below show the area fraction of all the pores in each interval relative to the total area of the section. All the relative frequency plots in the top row show exponential decay from a peak near zero so the smallest pores are most abundant and scarcity increases with pore size in all sections. However, the relative area fraction plots below show much of the porosity is contained in a few larger pores. No pores larger than 400 lm were found in any of the sections, but the distributions confirm that large pores are found in all sections as was shown in Fig. 2.

All the bottom plots also contain a single peak, but these peaks are shifted to size values substantially greater than zero. The lack of multiple peaks makes it difficult to distinguish between types of porosity (such as keyhole mode and lack of fusion pores) by size alone.

In Fig. 4, the pore size is plotted against the cumulative area fraction of pores in each section. To account for pores too small to be analysed (<5 lm), linear regression of pores smaller than 30 lm was used to calculate the required offsets for the curves to tend to zero. All four sections have similarly shaped curves in the figure. The cumulative area fraction porosity rises rapidly with pore size at first, but later converges toward a horizontal asymptote. The total area fraction porosity in each section is labelled in the figure, and this value is clearly near the associated asymptote. The horizontal sample's horizontal section (HH) was the most porous and Fig. 4 shows this is due to a relative abundance of larger pores. The least porous section was the vertical sample's horizontal section (VH), which was found to have relatively few pores of all sizes. The variation in porosity between sections can be caused by a number of factors. The laser window lens, gas filter and powder recoater blade all degrade with time during the LPBF process. Such degradation will affect part quality unevenly both over the build plate and in the build direction, leading to quality variations between samples.

Pore aspect ratio is plotted against pore size in Fig. 5. For small pores (<30 lm), the data is affected by image resolution as maximum aspect ratio increases with the number of pixels describing the pore. For larger pores, the maximum aspect ratio decreases with increasing size. However, sorting the data into 20 lm size intervals and taking the mean value of each interval reveals a different trend as shown by the black line labelled 'Average'. The average aspect ratio is stable for all pore sizes and orientations. Thus, the apparent decrease in aspect ratio with size reflects increasing scarcity of larger pores. Average aspect ratio numbers in Table 2 are calculated from pores larger than 30 lm in the samples. However, as sectioning always occurs at an angle to the major axis of pores the aspect ratio is systematically underestimated.

The angle between the major axis of a pore and the build plane is plotted against size for all pores in vertical sections (HV and VV) in Fig. 6. Angles are in the range 0-90 • where 0 • represents horizontal pores aligned with the layer boundaries and 90 • represents vertical pores aligned with the build direction. Grouping the data into 20 lm size intervals reveals the average angle decreases with pore size. The smallest pores (<20 lm) may appear evenly distributed in all orientations, but the grouped data indicates preference for horizontal alignment with an average angle of 34 • instead of 45 • as would be expected from a random distribution. The preference becomes stronger with increasing pore size. The standard deviation from the average values was 23 • and 20 • for HV and VV respectively, and 89% of pores larger than 100 lm were aligned within 45 • of the build plane. Therefore, despite scatter in the data there is a tendency for large pores to be oriented horizontally along the layer boundaries.

## Porosity and microstructure of as-built material

Fig. 7 presents the microstructure of as-built LPBF 316L material. The microstructure is consistent with LPBF microstructures characterised elsewhere in literature. Melt pool boundaries are visible and the rotating scanning strategy is evident from the different melt pool shapes. 'Layer-layer' melt pool boundaries identify the line of fusion between layers, while 'track-track' boundaries identify the edge of overlap to an adjacent scan track. Columnar grains of various sizes are generally oriented toward the build direction and frequently grow through melt pool boundaries. Grains can terminate abruptly at boundaries, but most meet other grains inside melt pools as expected from competitive growth. Each grain contains a cellular structure with low-angle boundaries as shown in the SEM micrograph in Fig. 7b. Most large pores are found on layer boundaries, particularly at junctions where a layer-layer boundary meets a track-track boundary.

Fig. 8 shows etched surfaces of LPBF 316L produced with no rotation between layers. A section normal to the scanning direction (SD) is presented in Fig. 8a which shows the microstructure consists of melt pools lying directly on top of each other. The view is rotated 90 • about the build direction in Fig. 8b where the melt pools are sectioned in the scanning direction normal to the hatching direction (HD). The lack of fusion pores have different geometries in the two sections. In Fig. 8a, the pores are small with low aspect ratio and are located at junctions of track-track and layer-layer boundaries. In the side view shown in Fig. 8b, the pores are elongated along the layer-layer boundaries. Such lack of fusion pore geometry have been observed elsewhere in literature.

Various types of insufficient melt pool overlap are shown in Fig. 9. The meander scanning strategy with no rotation between layers is assumed. Fig. 9a shows the front view with the scanning direction out of the plane. A normal melt pool section is shown to the left which has good overlap with surrounding melt pools. The three melt pools to the right have abnormal shapes leading to areas with no overlap marked in red, similar to work done by Tang et al.. Low energy density (ED) may produce a melt pool too small to sufficiently overlap with neighbouring melt pools. However, excessive energy density can cause evaporation in the melt pool and the classic keyhole shape. Such melt pools have deep penetration, but the shape may cause insufficient overlap with adjacent melt pools as shown in the figure. The shape on the right shows a disrupted melt pool. Instability may be caused by a number of factors including surface tension variations, spatter and inclusions. The latter represented by a green particle in the figure. All the abnormal melt pool shapes in Fig. 9a form areas of insufficient overlap leading to lack of fusion. These relatively small areas have low aspect ratios in this section, but Fig. 9b shows another section rotated by 90 • about the build direction. When lack of fusion is initiated at a layer-layer melt pool boundary, it may be extended during the process in the scanning direction along the layer boundary. Therefore, the lack of fusion pores have high aspect ratios and preferred alignment with layer boundaries in the scanning direction. This theory is in agreement with the images shown in Fig. 8 as well as the findings from image analysis in Section 3.1 that lack of fusion pores have clear preference with regard to orientation relative to the build direction.

## Microstructural evolution with heat treatment

Figs. 10 and 11 show optical and SEM images respectively of samples heat treated at various temperatures. Looking only at the six optical micrographs in Fig. 10, it would appear the overall grain structure is not highly affected by heat treatment up to 1040 • C as it is only the 1200 • C sample that features a substantially different grain structure with much larger grains and annealing twins. However, the SEM images in Fig. 11 show that microstructural changes do occur at lower temperatures on a smaller scale. There is little evidence of new grain nucleation in the sample heat treated at 1200 • C and some traces of the as-built structure remain. While the microstructures presented in Figs. 10 and 11 show resilience to grain growth up to 1040 • C, the melt pool boundaries gradually disappear at lower temperatures. Such boundaries are thin bands of slightly different composition to the melt pool interior. Their presence after heat treatment suggests little atomic diffusion was induced while their dissolution is evidence of significant diffusion. The melt pool boundaries appear largely unaffected by heat treatment at 700 • C, but at 800 • C they become thinner and less distinguishable from grain boundaries. The contrast between the melt pool boundary and interior is also reduced. After heat treatment at 900 • C, the melt pool boundaries have clearly started to dissolve and only vague traces are evident after heat treatment at 1040 • C. Atomic diffusion therefore gradually becomes significant over the temperature range 700-1040 • C for 60 min heat treatments. This is substantiated by the dissolution of subgranular cellular structures with increasing heat treatment temperature shown by the SEM images in Fig. 11. Cell walls consist of higher dislocation density and higher concentrations of heavy elements relative to (a) Horizontally built samples (b) Vertically built samples cell interiors, both of which can provide contrast in backscattered electron (BSE) SEM images. Fig. 11 shows the cellular structure dissolves over a similar heat treatment temperature range as the melt pool boundaries (700-1040 • C). This is reasonable as both cell walls and melt pool boundaries are chemical segregations.

When chemical segregations are dissolved by diffusion the grains become homogeneous. Controlling the heat treatment temperature and time can therefore adjust the homogeneity of the material. The samples heat treated at 1200 • C in Figs. 10 and 11 feature some evidence of pitting corrosion assumed to be caused by the specimen preparation. Otherwise, the grains have been fully homogenised by the annealing heat treatment as all traces of the cells have been dissolved.

## Yield behaviour evolution vs heat treatment

The curves in Fig. 12 present data up to the onset of necking in horizontal and vertical build orientations. The elongation at break was greater for horizontal samples than vertical samples on average for all heat treatments. However, there was significant variability between samples of each condition except for as-built vertical samples which showed consistent poor ductility (0.5-3.2% elongation at break). The majority of samples present low ductility compared to values of 30-60% quoted in literature. This low ductility is attributed to the relatively high level of porosity in the material.

Yield strength is plotted against heat treatment temperature in clear anisotropy as all horizontal samples start yielding at higher stresses than all vertical samples (19% greater on average). However, the strength of all as-built samples (in both orientations) was more than twice that reported for fully annealed 316L material (170 MPa ) represented by the line labelled 'Fully annealed' in Fig. 13. This line is horizontal because a fully annealed microstructure is unaffected by further heat treatment.

Figs. 12 and 13 show monotonic reduction of average yield strength with increasing heat treatment temperature in both build orientations. However, as shown by the converging curves in Fig. 13 the anisotropy diminishes with increasing heat treatment temperature. The average difference between horizontal and vertical sample yield strengths was reduced from 19% in the as-built condition to 8% after heat treatment at 700 • C. The average values for samples heat treated at 1200 • C were almost identical in both orientations, suggesting the material was transformed through heat treatment to become isotropic with regard to yield strength.

Porosity in the material was unaffected by any of the heat treatments as they were conducted at atmospheric pressure and all holding temperatures were well below the melting range of 316L. Since the yield anisotropy was eliminated by heat treatment, this means the cause must be microstructural and not related to porosity. The curves shown in Fig. 13 resemble work by Clarebrough et al. relating electrical resistivity and hardness to heat treatment temperature. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) was used to measure the release of stored energy during annealing of deformed metals and two distinctive energy peaks were identified. A lower temperature peak was related to dislocation annihilation and a higher temperature peak was related to recrystallisation. Both peaks coincided with a reduction in electrical resistivity, and the electrical resistivity vs annealing temperature plots look very similar to the curves in Fig. 13 where two drops in yield strength are observed. The first is a small drop at lower heat treatment temperature (700-800 • C) and the second is a larger drop at higher temperature (1040-1200 • C).

Optical and SEM images in Figs. 10 and 11 show no clear microstructural changes between as-built samples and those heat treated at 700 • C, but the reduction in yield strength shown in Fig. 13 suggests some reduction in dislocation density. In conventional material processing, cold working hardens a material by increasing the dislocation density while heat treatments reducing the dislocation density are referred to as 'recovery'. Although LPBF materials are generated in a state of high dislocation density, the term 'recovery' may be useful to describe heat treatments that reduce dislocation density.

Different background colours are used in Fig. 13 to categorise heat treatments into regimes based on microstructural changes. Figs. 10 and 11 show atomic diffusion becomes significant between 700 • C and 800 • C, so heat treatments up to 750 • C are part of the 'Recovery' regime of Fig. 13. The main microstructural change of such heat treatments is a reduction in dislocation density. In the same manner, Figs. 10 and 11 show substantial grain growth first begins at a temperature between 1040 • C and 1200 • C. The temperature range from 1120 • C to the beginning of the melting range (1371 • C ) is therefore called as the 'Annealing' regime where significant grain growth occurs. Between recovery and annealing is the 750-1120 • C range called the 'Homogenisation'. Heat treatments in this regime induce atomic diffusion to dissolve microsegregations such as cell walls and melt pool boundaries. Note that the temperature ranges of the recovery, homogenisation and annealing regimes are not measured precisely in this investigation and will change with the holding time and cooling rate of the heat treatment.

The right side of Fig. 13 illustrates the approximate relative contributions of different microstructural features to the yield strength of as-built LPBF 316L. Fully annealed 316L has been reported to have a yield strength of 170 MPa, most of which can be attributed to lattice resistance to dislocation motion. Figs. 10 and 13 show substantial grain growth and reduced in yield strength between samples heat treated at 1040 • C and 1200 • C. Grain boundaries therefore provide significant strengthening to the material. Samples near the lower end of the homogenisation regime (700 • C) were stronger than those near the upper end (1040 • C), so chemical segregations also provide considerable further strengthening. The remaining strength of asbuilt material is attributed to dislocation density, which was partially relieved by the recovery heat treatment at 700 • C.

All three strengthening mechanisms as well as crystal texture contribute to yield strength anisotropy. If the grain structure is textured, the average Schmidt factor will vary with the direction of loading. The columnar grains are aligned with the build direction so the number of grain boundaries a dislocation has to overcome will vary with the loading direction. Likewise, cells tend to grow from melt pool boundaries upwards toward the melt pool centre. This causes cell walls (chemical segregation) to prefer alignment with the build direction making their strength contribution anisotropic as well. Finally, the dislocation density at any location in a part is affected by the thermal history of that point. The dislocation density may therefore be different in horizontal and vertical samples as heat buildup and cooling conditions will be different.

Another source of strengthening suggested in literature is nanoparticles (chromium oxides and silicates) which have been observed at cell walls. Such particles have a hardening effect and would not be affected by heat treatment. However, their contribution has been calculated to be around 5-10 MPa, which would only account for around 2% of as-built material strength. Particle hardening is therefore less significant than grain boundary strengthening, chemical segregation and dislocation density for strengthening LPBF 316L.

## Ductility and failure behaviour

Elongation at break is plotted against heat treatment temperature for all samples in Fig. 14. Horizontal samples are consistently much more ductile than vertical samples, which indicates there are features in the material impervious to heat treatment that make it anisotropic with regard to ductility. In addition, and despite significant scatter in the data of both orientations, increasing trends between heat treatment temperature and ductility may be inferred as well (the positive slopes of the regression lines). This suggests microstructural changes caused by heat treatment also contribute to increasing the ductility of the material. The most obvious cause of consistent differences in ductility is porosity. However, the analysis described in Section 3.1 found horizontal samples were more porous than vertical samples (0.61% vs 0.31% respectively). Relative density is therefore not always an accurate indicator of ductility. The analysis found pores were larger in horizontal samples and such large pores preferred alignment with layer boundaries in both horizontal and vertical samples. Fig. 15 illustrates how the angle between the direction of loading and the major axis of the pore (the longest dimension) can vary from 0 • to 90 •. From a structural integrity point of view, the least favourable angle is 90 • as shown in Fig. 15b where stress is applied normal to the major axis of a pore. This configuration maximises the stress concentrations at the apexes of the pore to induce crack initiation or ductile void growth. Compare this to Fig. 15c where stress is applied parallel to the major axis (h = 0 • ). This configuration minimises stress concentrations and requires greater load to initiate void growth.

Fig. 16 shows how the angle between pore orientation (major axis) and direction of loading differs in horizontal and vertical samples built using 67 • rotation about the build direction between layers.

Three successive layers are shown in each sample, and every layer contains a lack of fusion pore elongated in the scanning direction along the layer boundary. For the vertical sample in Fig. 16a, the direction of loading is normal to all the pores because the load is applied normal to the layer boundaries. However, in the horizontal sample shown in Fig. 16b the angle varies from 0 • to 90 • between layers due to the 67 • rotating scanning strategy. The angle is particularly unfavourable every 8 th layer when h = 90 ± 4 • (because 67 • 8 = 90 • 6 -4).

The images in Fig. 2 show the porosity is not evenly distributed, but instead forms clusters in certain areas. This is highlighted in Fig. 17 where etched sections of as-built samples are displayed. Note in particular the inset of Fig. 17b where large pores have formed in a line. The scanning direction is rotated by 90 • on either side of this line, indicating it is the edge of a square from the chessboard scanning strategy employed. Such clusters of large lack of fusion pores on a single layer may explain why some vertical samples failed at very low strains. If such a random distribution of pores over the section is representative of the material as a whole, then ductility is largely determined by whether large pores are unfavourably clustered and oriented relative to the loading direction. This explains the large variability in ductility between samples subjected to the same heat treatment, reflected in the scatter of the data in Fig. 14.

## Analysis of fracture subsurface material

Fig. 18 presents an etched section of a vertical as-built sample tested to failure occurring at 1.46% elongation. The fracture surface is almost perfectly normal to the direction of loading as fracture took place within just 200 lm or four 50 lm layers. Sintered powder particles are visible across the surface, indicative of multiple lack of fusion pores within the same layer. Meanwhile, the microstructure immediately below the surface is virtually indistinguishable from unstressed as-built material, suggesting significant ductile deformation was limited to material very close to the fracture surface. The implication of these observations is that fracture occurred by coalescence of lack of fusion pores by crack growth along the layer boundaries. The inset in Fig. 18 shows the crack path was affected by the local microstructure. Much of the fracture surface follows layer-layer melt pool boundaries, while sudden shifts in the surface profile occur at junctions where melt pool boundaries meet (labelled 'boundary junction' in the figure).

The equivalent section of a horizontal as-built sample is shown in Fig. 19. This sample was more ductile failing at 25.9% elongation. The melt pool boundaries are clearly visible, showing the melt pools are stretched in the loading direction throughout the gauge length. As with the vertical sample, the fracture surface has clearly connected multiple lack of fusion pores. However, the profile between them is not as straight. This is in agreement with the void growth mechanism illustrated in Figs. 15 and 16. The orientation of porosity relative to the direction of loading encourages more ductile failure behaviour.

The positive slopes of the trendlines in Fig. 14 suggest heat treatment induced microstructural changes to improve ductility. Fig. 20 shows heat treated samples (800 • C and 1200 • C) tested to failure and sectioned to revealed the microstructure below the fracture surface. All heat treated samples display more ductile behaviour than their as-built counterparts as the fracture surfaces are less orthogonal to the loading direction. However, the heat treated samples also show evidence that porosity coalescence leading to failure. The microstructural effects on failure behaviour in these samples were consequently of limited significance.

## Implications for quality assurance and heat treatment of structural parts

Results from this study have found porosity dominates failure behaviour in LPBF 316L parts. Material porosity cannot be completely eliminated, but may be managed by optimising process parameters and other process systems such as gas flow and powder feeding to reduce the frequency of large pore formation in the LPBF process. For qualification purposes the Archimedes method is of limited use as it does not describe the size, shape, orientation or distribution of pores. Instead, non-destructive qualification processes such as X-ray microtomography or in-situ process monitoring techniques may be required to qualify parts for critical applications.

As-built LPBF 316L was found to be strong in both horizontal and vertical build orientations, but vertical samples consistently showed low ductility (0.5-3.2%). This is concerning with regard to structural integrity as these samples were also particularly vulnerable to failure by crack growth along layer-layer melt pool boundaries to connect pores on the same layer. Heat treatment may decrease this vulnerability. Recovery heat treatments can reduce dislocation density to increase ductility, or homogenisation treatments may reduce the anisotropy of both yield and failure behaviour. However, further research is required to evaluate the effects of heat treatments on other material properties before any recommendation can be made.

## Conclusions

In this study heat treatment was used as an investigative tool to isolate the influence of porosity and microstructural features on the mechanical properties of 316L parts produced by LPBF. The investigation led to the following conclusions:

• Porosity vs yield behaviour: Porosity does not cause anisotropic yield behaviour. This was demonstrated by heat treatment as isotropic yield behaviour was recovered with increasing heat treatment temperature. Since the pores are unaffected by heat treatment, the cause of yield anisotropy must be microstructural.

• Porosity vs failure behaviour: A positive and directionally dependent correlation was found between porosity and ductility. Horizontally built samples, despite higher average levels of porosity, were more ductile than vertically built samples. This was explained by the shape and orientation of pores relative to the loading direction. Most porosity was contained in a few large lack of fusion defects. These high aspect ratio pores had preferential orientation along layer boundaries between adjacent scan tracks. Analysis of fracture subsurface material found failure in both horizontal and vertical loading directions involved coalescence of large pores in the material.

• Microstructure vs yield behaviour: Microstructural features were found to greatly influence yield strength of as-built material. Heat treatment, microscopy and tensile testing results were combined to reveal microstructural strengthening mechanisms. In addition to the inherent lattice resistance to dislocation motion, the material was strengthened by grain boundary strengthening, chemical segregation along melt pool boundaries and cell walls, as well as heterogeneous dislocation density within the material. All three strengthening mechanisms may contribute to anisotropic yield behaviour.

• Microstructure vs failure behaviour: Failure behaviour was dominated by porosity, but analysis of fracture subsurface material found evidence of microstructural influence as well.

As-built vertical samples failed by ductile crack growth along layer-layer melt pool boundaries to connect lack of fusion pores. Coalescence of pores was also found in horizontal samples, but the failure connected pores spread further apart in the direction of loading necessitating more ductile crack growth. Heat treatments dissolving melt pool boundaries increased ductility in both orientations, but anisotropic ductility remains due to the orientation of pores.

• Heat treatment for practical applications: Heat treatment was categorised into three regimes; recovery, homogenisation, and annealing. For structural parts, heat treatment may be required to improve ductility. This study found promising results for reducing dislocation density by heat treatment without sacrificing the strengthening contributions of the as-built grain structure and cellular substructure.

This study has shown that whilst relative density is a useful indicator of part quality, it is not alone sufficient to evaluate the structural integrity of LPBF parts. The shape, size, orientation and distribution of pores are crucial parameters affecting mechanical properties. Methods are needed to detect and measure these parameters in order to assure the structural integrity of LPBF parts.

title: An investigation over microstructure and HIP processing effects on wear performance of pure chromium parts fabricated by laser powder bed fusion
body_text:
ABSTRACT

texture Hot isostatic pressing Wear performance A B S T R A C T Chromium (Cr) and its alloys have long been valued for their exceptional properties, including corrosion resistance and high-temperature stability, rendering them indispensable in industrial applications such as chemical processing, energy production, and aerospace. However, due to the difficulties in Cr-based alloy manufacturing, there is a need for novel manufacturing methodologies. Additive Manufacturing (AM) emerges as a promising approach, particularly Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF), which allows for intricate designs, reduced material waste, and simplified assembly. However, certain issues still need to be addressed, including defects like cracks and porosities in the manufactured parts. Post-processing techniques such as Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) have gained prominence for enhancing the material properties and quality of AM parts, including those produced using LPBF. HIP treatments are effective in eliminating internal pores, although some challenges remain, notably the presence of trapped argon and grain coarsening side effects of HIP process parameters. This study focuses on LPBF-processed pure chromium parts with crystallographic texture and investigates their properties after HIP treatment, including microstructure, hardness, and tribological performance. According to the obtained results: the HIP process reduced cracks, especially in the center region, but increased gaps in the side region. HIP also hindered grain realignment, limiting grain growth, and resulting in high HAGB density and low MUD values. Elevated HIP processing pressure negatively affected tribological performance due to increased grain size, and reduced hardness. This study, for the first time, realized the effect of HIP conditions on the microstructure and tribological performance of LPBF-processed pure Cr.

BODY

## Introduction

Chromium and its alloys play a significant role in industrial applications due to their exceptional properties. Their corrosion resistance and high-temperature stability make them ideal for harsh environments like chemical processing, energy production, and aerospace. Hightemperature working performance with lower-density Cr provides an alternative solution where Nickel-based superalloys may not suffice to address certain needs. Up to date, Cr has been used as a coating or alloying element in steel, thanks to its performance against corrosion, and low friction coefficient. However, manufacturing technologies and characterization studies are still needed to obtain highperformance Cr-based final products to address industrial requirements.

The manufacturing of Cr via conventional methodologies is challenging due to the high melting point with limited ductility at room temperature. The casting process needs to be done over 1900 • C and its plastic deformation is also difficult due to its high ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (BDTT) under forming loads. At this point, Additive Manufacturing (AM) offers advantages for Cr-based final product manufacturing. Complex geometries can be easily manufactured while decreasing the total weight via topology optimization. Besides these merits, the reduction in material waste and simplified assembly are other appealing aspects of Cr-based alloys AM for green manufacturing. Because the Cr-based alloy conventional manufacturing process is usually a major source of pollution.

As an AM method, laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) has attracted attention with the capability to manufacture near-net shape parts, coupled with reduced production durations and the method ensures the sustainability of raw materials. Besides these advantages, studies are still needed to improve LPBF-processed Cr-based parts. LPBF is an innovative AM technology that employs a laser beam as a heat source to directly shape the loaded product geometry data by melting specific metal powders layer-by-layer. The laser is precisely focused on an average 100 μm spot size (standard laser diameter for EOS M290 LPBF machine) reaching over 3000 • C, however, defects like cracks, and porosities in asbuilt components were reported previously. Besides, the process parameters such as laser power, scanning speed, hatch spacing, and powder properties can initiate or mitigate defect formation. To minimize the defects, short scan lengths and a high energy density approach have been implemented in this study according to successful findings in previous studies while the built stage was preheated to 200 • C to decrease the residual stress. Even though precautions during the LPBF fabrication process have been implemented, porosities, surface-internal cracks, distortions and delaminations, stair-case effects on surface topography, and adhesion of unfused powder particles are some inevitable quality issues. Especially during the LPBF manufacturing of pure Cr severe cracking phenomena were observed due to the mismatch of residual stresses and low BDTT.

Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP), heat treatments, hot forming, laser postprocessing remelting methods, and their combinations are being applied as post-processes to increase material properties and quality of AM parts. Beyond other methods, HIP is widely being investigated especially for LPBF-produced components. With the effect of high temperature and pressure, the internal pores of the 3D part can be eliminated. Due to the nature of the HIP process, there are remaining internal pores as a result of trapped Argon.

Due to the superior properties of Cr, there is a need for improvements in novel manufacturing methodologies. This study investigated the LPBF fabrication of hard-to-process pure Cr which has high DBTT, therefore LPBF processing of pure Cr has been quite challenging. Previous studies have reported LPBF process parameter optimization and decreasing scan length to accumulate heat to overcome cracks and improve the component density. However, the current literature lacks an understanding of the effect of the HIP process on the defects and microstructure of pure Cr fabricated by the LPBF process and its wear performance. In order to obtain high-quality Cr-based final parts, crystallographic textured LPBF-processed pure Cr cubes were manufactured and the HIP process was applied to understand its effect on material properties. The microstructural investigation, hardness, and tribological performances were analyzed before and after HIP treatment to understand the influence of HIP process parameters.

## Materials method

## LPBF processing of pure Cr

Irregular shape pure Cr powder (>99% purity, JFE Material, Japan) was used to fabricate 5 × 5 × 5 mm cube samples by LPBF (Fig. 1(b)). Even though Cr was processed by a cost-efficient method, resulting in an irregular shape, the particle size distribution (D50 = 44.8 μm) and powder flowability with an avalanche angle and a surface fractal of 52.8 • and 1.95, respectively, were suitable for the LPBF process.

LPBF fabrication of pure Cr samples was performed on a 316 L stainless steel base plate by EOS M290 (Germany) LPBF machine equipped with a 400 W Yb laser with a 100 μm diameter. The optimized LPBF process parameters according to our previous study, layer thickness (h), laser power (P), scan speed (V), and hatch spacing (d), were chosen as 20 μm, 150 W, 400 mm/s, and 80 μm, respectively, with the preheating of build stage to 200 • C (Table 1). The volume energy density (E) of LPBF processing can be calculated by Eq. ( 1).

## Hot isostatic pressing

The HIP parameters were selected as 1250 • C and two different pressures (100 MPa and 200 MPa). Here the aim was to understand the pressure effect at high temperature. The effect of HIP process on internal porosities was controlled via a non-destructive Achimedes' principle testing method (ASTM B962 Standard). Weight Lab balance was used which was equipped with a density measurement device for solid materials. The density measurement test was made in alcohol at room temperature with a measurement accuracy of 0.001 g. This methodology neglects the effect of central defects. To investigate defects, image processing techniques were employed from optical microscope images.

## Microstructural characterization

Optical images (OM images) were captured perpendicular to the LPBF build direction (Fig. 1, x-z plane). The sample surfaces were initially polished using 320-2500 grit sandpaper. Subsequently, the polishing process was initiated using a 1 μm polishing cloth and a 0.01 μm alumina solution. For cleaning, the samples were immersed in ethyl alcohol within an ultrasonic cleaning device and then prepared for etching. The samples were etched using a reagent containing 20 ml of nitric acid and 60 ml of hydrochloric acid. They were left in this reagent for 60 s before being prepared for imaging with an optical microscope. Optical microscopy was employed for the analysis of defect percentages and microstructure. The acquired OM images were processed using ImageJ software to determine the density of each sample based on the defect area ratio within the section. Defects (cracks, lack of fusion, and porosities) were calculated as a percentage of the measured area. Measurements were taken from the surface of each specimen with an area of 780 × 580 μm. Four measurements were repeatedly performed, and the averages with standard deviations of these measurements were calculated. To assess the impact of the HIP process on the sample and to understand the defects within it, cross-sections were extracted from the middle of the sample for further investigations (Fig. 1).

The microstructure of as-build and HIPed Cr was examined using an electron backscatter diffraction system (EBSD, Nordlys Max3 system, Oxford Instruments, Cambridge, UK) mounted on a field-emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM; JIB-4610 F, JEOL, Tokyo, Japan) operated with at an accelerating voltage of 20 kV and a step size of 2 μm. The collected data was analyzed using analysis software (HKL Channel5, Oxford Instruments, UK) to obtain inverse pole figure (IPF) maps, corresponding pole figures, grain size distribution, grain boundary misorientation, qualitative and quantitative analyses of high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) and Kernel average misorientation (KAM) distribution.

## Hardness and Tribological characterizations

The hardness measurements of the samples were measured with Vickers Hardness Tester. Five different measurements were taken by applying 500 g of force, from the different parts of the surface of each sample. Then their means and standard deviations were found by statistical methods.

A radial cycle motion against a ceramic ball as counterface material was used to conduct the wear studies with Tribotester (Tribo Technic) machine. Al 2 O 3 ceramic ball (6 mm in diameter) had a Vickers hardness of 1800 Hv and was used as an abrasive during the tests. A normal load of 1 N was applied at a rotational speed of 20 mm/s under dry conditions. For the 6366.21 cycle of 40 m test length, the wear track radius was 1 mm. Abrasive balls were maintained firmly in accordance with ASTM G99-05 specifications. Surface topographies and wear track width were observed by FE-SEM (Thermo Scientific) investigations. FE-SEM Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS) mapping was also applied to identify wear mechanisms. 10 repetitive width measurements were done to calculate the mean value. Wear volume loss calculated according to Eq. ( 2).

As-built Cr reached 6.95 g/cm 3 density, which indicated 97.2% relative density compared to the 7.15 g/cm 3 theoretical density of pure chromium. The applied HIP process at 1250 • C with the pressure of 100 MPa (Cr-1250-100) increased the density to 7.01 /cm 3 (98.1% relative density), indicating a decrease in defects. Although the surface defects increased with the HIP process at 1250 • C with a pressure of 100 MPa, the center and the side region defects of Cr-1250-100 decreased (Fig. 1, Table 3). However, increasing the HIP pressure to 200 MPa the density of Cr-1250-200 decreased to 6.67 g/cm 3 (93.3% relative density), as such defects also increased overall.

## Results

## Microstructure of LPBF-processed and HIPed pure Cr components

Considering the densification and defect ratio of as-built and HIPed samples, hardness differed significantly. The highest hardness (195.29 ± 16.52 Hv) was measured from as-built and it decreased after the HIP process. The hardness of Cr-1250-100 samples was 154.58 ± 8.70 Hv. Despite the increase in density and decrease in defects, the hardness of Cr-1250-100 reduced due to the decrease in residual stress after the HIP process and the increase in grain size resulting in a decrease in HAGB density (Table 23). Increasing the HIP pressure from 100 MPa to 200 MPa further decreased the hardness. Although the HAGB density of Cr-1250-200 was comparable to that of as-built Cr, Cr-1250-200 exhibited lower hardness (144.37 ± 19.16 Hv), which contradicted Hall-Petch strengthening. However, this outcome can be attributed to the low density and higher porosity of the Cr-1250-200 sample.

Fig. 3 presents IPF and HAGB maps with the corresponding {001} pole figures of as-built and HIPed Cr samples. The IPF map of as-built Cr showed epitaxial grain growth reaching multiple powder layers (Fig. 3 (a)). The 〈001〉 grain orientation was strongly selected along y direction (x-z plane) while unstable/ rotated <001> grains can be identified from the pole figure, identified with the misorientation between build direction (z) and scan direction (x) (Fig. 3(a``)), resulting in 3.8 MUD (mean uniform density) which indicates the texture strength. Epitaxially grown grains and randomly oriented grains can be detected with the different colors (representing grain orientations) on IPF maps and grain boundaries are indicated with red lines on HAGB maps (Fig. 3).

Depending on the applied pressure of the HIP process, grain orientation, and HAGB distributions exhibited different characteristics (Fig. 3 (b, c)). Large and elongated grains with <001> (red) and 〈101〉 (green) orientations were detected in the IPF map of Cr-1250-100 (Fig. 3(b)) with an increase in relative intensity of MUD (3.9), allowing the intensities of non-ideal orientations to fade while the predominant grain orientation to remain, resulting fewer HAGBs. However, the increase in applied pressure during the HIP process for Cr-1250-200 samples prevented realignment of grain orientation and limited the grain growth, thus, resulting in high HAGB density and low MUD value.

The qualitative observations in Fig. 3 are quantified and presented in Fig. 4. The grain size distribution (Fig. 4(a)) and the misorientation distribution of HAGBs (Fig. 4(b)) proved the differences in microstructure of as-built and HIPed samples as well as the differences caused by the applied HIP pressure. The average grain size of Cr-1250-100 was 22.6 μm, which was higher than the as-built Cr grain size (16.3 μm). The grain growth dynamics also eliminated less misoriented HAGBs while realigning the small grains with the adjacent grains. However, the application of high-pressure (200 MPa) during the HIP process (Cr-1250-200) showed limited grain growth (19.6 μm) while primarily realizing grain growth within the less misoriented grains. Therefore, the shift of HAGB misorientation from a lower angle (15-25 • ) to a higher angle (45-60 • ) was observed (Fig. 4(b)).

The accumulated strain due to the fabrication condition and the stress-release effect of the HIP process can be estimated with the KAM values. Fig. 5 represents electron microscopy images of as-built and HIPed Cr with corresponding KAM maps. The as-built Cr sample exhibited high residual stress, indicated by the KAM color map (Fig. 5 (a')). Crack initiation and propagation could be identified in Fig. 5(a-c), corresponding to the location of high misorientation on KAM maps Fig. 5 (a'-c'). The KAM color maps of HIPed Cr samples indicated a release of residual stress as showing a decrease in KAM values. While the misorientation along the columnar grain boundary parallel to the build direction was observed from Cr 1250-100 (Fig. 5(b')), applying higher HIP pressure altered the grain structure and also affected KAM distribution (Fig. 5(c')). The quantitative analyses of KAM values were presented in Fig. 5(d) as a distribution of misorientation angle. The tendency of KAM distribution was shifted to lower values with HIP application. The descending order of average KAM values was as-built Cr (2.09) > Cr 1250-200 (1.14) > Cr 1250-100 (1.04), calculated from KAM angle distribution (Fig. 5(d)). According to this KAM distribution and the average values, slightly higher KAM was detected from Cr 1250-200 than Cr 1250-100, estimating that the high HIP pressure accumulated and/or kept stress remained in the structure.

## Wear properties

Table 4 gives the mean coefficient of friction (CoF), wear volume, and wear track widths. Fig. 5 (a, b) shows the plots of the CoF against the number of cycles on LPBF-processed pure Cr parts, respectively, under the 1 N and 5 N loading conditions. In the 5 N loading condition, the CoF fluctuated between 0.2 and 0.8. For tests with the 1 N loading condition, the CoF fluctuated between 0.8 and 1.5. Except for the as-built Cr sample, all the CoF data increased and reached the highest value then decreased and passed a more steady state deviation. The Cr 1250-100 sample exhibited a higher value of CoF scatter under 1 N and 5 N loading (Fig. 6 a, b). Fig. 6 shows that the variation of the CoF against the number of strokes for the Cr 1250-200 has a steady character with the highest value scattering within 0.9-1.3 (Fig. 6 a). In the (Fig. 6), under 1 N loading condition higher mean CoF values were recorded (Fig. 6 Table 4). The lowest CoF was recorded in the as-built state under 5 N loading condition with 0.26. The highest CoF was recorded in the Cr-1250-100 group with 1.12, and 0.66 for 1 N and 5 N load, respectively. The wear volumes were calculated from mean wear track width measurements according to the Eq. ( 1). Parallel to CoF values, the lowest wear volumes were recorded as-build state with 0.22 and 1.13 respectively for 1 N and 5 N loading conditions (Table 4). Due to the effect of the HIP process higher wear volume loss was recorded. Cr 1250-200 had 1.8, and 4.14 for the 1 N and 5 N loading conditions, respectively. Besides having the highest CoF value, Cr 1250-100 samples resulted in moderate wear volume with 0.48, and 2.72 for the 1 N and 5 N loading conditions, respectively. Fig. 7 shows the wear morphologies and EDS map of the wear tracks under 5 N load conditions. Adhered particles and cracks emerged with delamination in all the grooves under a 5 N force, causing damage to the columnar structures that are oriented perpendicular to the sliding direction due to applied high stress. In all cases, the fractured and adhered particles were observed besides the adhered craters produced due to ploughing. The significant damage observed on the surfaces points towards cracking and ploughing as the predominant wear mechanisms involved.

## Discussion

## The effect of HIP parameters on microstructure

As-built Cr contained serious cracking issues, of which some were open to the surface while some were closed. These cracks were identified as solidification cracks, which occurred due to the fast-cooling rate of the LPBF process resulting in high residual stress. With the fast cooling to room temperature, the residual stress reached over yield strength of as-built Cr, thus resulting in cracks along the HAGBs. The HIP process has been applied to improve part density with the application of high temperature and pressure in a short processing time.

The application of HIP to as-built Cr in this study differed in terms of densification, hardness, microstructure, and wear performance of Cr parts regarding the difference in applied pressure. After LPBF, besides cracks, porosities also were observed in x-z plane (Fig. 2). To understand the changes in the build direction, x-y plane was also observed and similar findings were observed (Fig. 8). Low-pressure HIP process (Cr-1250-100) improved the density and decreased internal defects while open-surface defects increased. Because HIP was ineffective for open pores and defects. Moreover, high HIP pressure was detrimental to the density of Cr components, resulting in lower density than the as-built Cr sample while increasing the ratio of defects. The high HIP pressure was expected to promote crack growth and jeopardize the densification. This was estimated considering the high HIP pressure showing higher KAM distribution than Cr 1250-100, indicating high residual stress, thus, resulting increase in defects and decrease in density.

HIP is one of the major post densification method with the combined effect of high temperature and pressure together. Besides, high densification levels could be achieved when sintering pre-alloyed or pure prealloyed metal combinations, sintering, parameter optimization, powder sizes, and selection of elemental composition are other methods to modulate density. The comprehensive examination of processing parameters, with a particular emphasis on energy density, has been carried out to assess their influence on the densification levels of metal parts fabricated through partial melting AM. As an example of powder particle size and sintering temperature effect, in, the density of S316 stainless steel varied between 98 and 67%. In, Cubased samples were manufactured with a relative density higher than 99% using CuCr1.3 powder (wt%) through LPBF. The effect of laser scanning parameter were studied and 97% relative density was found for pure SLM printed Cu which found to be low for industrial applications. Simchi and Pohl maximized SLS fabricated iron based alloys relative density via sintering. In this current study, using the accepted density of pure Cr as 7.19 g/cm 3 from the periodic table, the densification percentages were measured as 96.66%, 97.49%, and 92.76% for the as-built Cr, Cr 1250-100, and Cr 1250-200 samples respectively. Previous studies have defined a high densification rate as <98%. In the Cr 1250-100 sample group, 97.49% relative density was closest to the high densification level.

The results of densification reflected the hardness of as-built and HIPed Cr samples. HIP application at high temperatures released the residual stress induced by the LPBF process, thus resulting in a decrease in the hardness of HIP samples. However, the HIP processes with different applied pressures differed in terms of the mechanism of hardening the sample. While Cr-1250-100 with a bigger grain size and fewer HAGBs had higher hardness than Cr-1250-200. The higher hardness was achieved owing to the improved densification and decrease in defects even though high HIP pressure (Cr 1250-200) exhibited high average KAM value. Cr-1250-200 had smaller grains and more HAGBs, the hardness value was the lowest among the samples due to low density and high ratio of defects. Therefore, it is important to note that the applied HIP pressure should be determined regarding the as-built condition of additively manufactured components, considering surface-opened defects. The HIP processing of as-built Cr with different pressures exhibited significant differences in microstructure characteristics. While LPBF processing of Cr formed texture via epitaxial grain growth along the preferential <001> direction parallel to the BD, Cr-1250-100 exhibited further texture strengthening. This mechanism is expected due to the formation of a more uniform microstructure with the alignment of small grains towards easy growth <001> crystallographic orientation which requires less energy and/or grain growth with realigning low energy HAGBs (such as lower misorientations and/or coincidence site lattice boundaries). While hardness value is accepted as an indicator of wear resistance, this study highlighted the importance of HIP condition on the hardness of additively manufactured pure Cr in terms of density/ defects and microstructural characteristics.

## The effect of HIP parameters on friction and wear performance

The as-built state resulted in the minimum, and Cr-1250-100 resulted in the highest CoF value. The main underlying reason is suspected as the HIP process temperature altering the material properties, affecting grain size, HAGB density and distribution, KAM distribution, and defect ratio. Regarding these microstructural differences, there was a %20 decrease in hardness after the 1250 • C and 100 MPa HIP process. This decrease was %26 after the 1250 • C and 200 MPa HIP process. As seen in the EBSD results, the increase in applied pressure during the HIP process prevented the realignment of grain orientation and restricted grain growth, thereby resulting in high HAGB density and a low MUD value while keeping the residual stress remained or accumulating stress due to high HIP pressure, which positively affected tribological performance relative to the 100 MPa sample.

For all samples and loading conditions CoF increased at initial sliding cycles. As sliding distance increased, fluctuations in the CoF decreased. These two behaviors were grouped as running in and steady stade stages which were shown as dashed lines in Fig. 6. The initial increase in the CoF was attributed smaller contact area between the abrasive ball and the sample surface due to the rougher surface. Further deviations grounded with the combined effect of abrasive-adhesive wear. HIP-applied samples resulted in higher deviations than the as-built state as shown in Fig. 6. deviations in the CoF were lower under 5 N load due to plastic deformation. The wear study of pure Cr is very limited. Previous tribological investigations have mainly focused on Cr coatings, with limited attention given to additively manufactured Cr based materials. , researchers used bulk pure Cr, and tested its tribological performance under 5 N loading conditions. The CoF value varied between 0.12 and 0.24 which agrees well with the measured CoF values of this study for the as-built state under the same loading condition (Table 3). CoF is strongly affected by the micro-macro structure of the material and tribology testing method. As-built samples had the lowest porosity with the highest hardness, residual stress, and CoF resulting in the smallest mean with the lowest fluctuations and CoF value. The highest fluctuations and CoF were observed with the lowest hardness and highest porosity (Cr-1250-200). The surface defects increase the roughness which causes high deviations in CoF as highlighted previously. Previously, additive manufactured Co-Cr-Mo with different Ti additions samples findings were parallel to and consistent with the current study. With a higher amount of Ti percentage, the hardness decreased and, the porous structure increased which initiated the rise in the CoF values.

Under the 1 N loading state, the CoF values varied between 0.679 and 1.129 against the ball. Friction behavior was strongly affected by the applied load and testing conditions. An increase in the applied load resulted in decreased CoFs to 0.26-0.56 intervals. Similar behavior was observed in previous studies. This decrease can be attributed to the increased interlocking between the abrasive ball and the sample's surface as a result of the higher normal load. This enhanced contact between the surfaces reduces resistance and facilitates relative sliding between the abrasive ball and the surface.

Three main wear mechanisms were observed in the observations: oxide formation, adhesions, and delamination. As seen in Fig. 9 (a-c) the oxide layer was observed on all samples. During the sliding an oxide layer formed between the surfaces, and due to the abrasive wear mechanism oxide layer-fractured particles accumulated in some regions. These adhered particles can be observed in Figs. 7 and 9 (black arrows). This re-adhered abraded particle creates peaks on the mating surface, leading to the formation of non-uniform wear patterns as shown in Fig. 9 with arrows. As seen in Figs. 7, and 9, the wear track's edge of samples was rough and Cr and O elements appeared in the EDS map. In all samples, oxygen was observed which points oxidative wear mechanism due to the effect of abrasion. In EDS maps element transition to the sample surfaces from Al 2 O 3 abrasive ball was not observed (Fig. 9).

## Conclusions

Experiments were conducted to assess the influence of HIP treatment on LPBF-processed, crystallographic-textured pure Cr specimens. The effect of the HIP pressure on the defects, microstructure, and mechanical properties is investigated using a systematic study, and the following is concluded:

• Application of the HIP process decreased the cracks, especially in the center regions of cubic samples. The increased pressure of the process decreased defects in the center region of the samples, however, increased in the surface region.

• An increase in applied pressure during the HIP process prevented the realignment of grain orientation and limited grain growth, resulting in a high HAGB density, high average KAM value, and a low MUD value.

• HIP processing pressure negatively affected tribological performance reasoned with grain growth and a reduction in hardness value, increased amount of surface porosities due to the temperature and pressure employed in the process.

• Increased HIP process pressure decreased the wear performance due to a high ratio of defects. Lower HIP process pressure strengthened the texture via realignment of neighboring grains with low misorientation along the preferential <001> direction parallel to the BD, which enabled better wear performance.

The results obtained, in demonstrating the impact of HIP on the microstructural and material properties of LPBF-manufactured, crystallographically textured samples, are noteworthy. Notably, an increase in HIP pressure has a positive effect on limiting grain growth, however, simultaneously leads to an increase in defects. To fully utilize this microstructural effect of HIP pressure, further investigations are warranted to achieve lower defect levels. Moreover, it is required to achieve highly dense structures through further optimization of the LPBF process (such as high preheat) and HIP conditions (high pressure for samples without surface defects) or by alloying to overcome the brittle nature of pure Cr. Additionally, the potential impact of applying 100 MPa HIP pressure at lower temperatures on defect reduction while avoiding grain growth should also be explored.
